body.en: Chapter 4's method needs \( g(x) \) built from polynomials, exponentials, and sines/cosines — its whole trial-and-match table only has entries for those. What about \( \tan x \), \( \sec x \), \( 1/x \), or \( \ln x \)? None of those show up on any list of trial forms, and no amount of multiplying by \( x \) fixes that — the method doesn't apply at all. This chapter builds a completely different technique that needs no trial, no table, and no resonance check: it finds a particular solution for any continuous \( g(x) \) whatsoever, built directly out of the two solutions Chapter 3 already found.

label.en: ● Definition 5.1 — The Wronskian of the complementary solutions

body.en: Let \( y_1,y_2 \) be the two linearly independent solutions of the associated homogeneous equation \( ay''+by'+cy=0 \) given by Theorem 3.2 (whichever of its three cases applies), so the complementary function is \( y_c=C_1y_1+C_2y_2 \). Their Wronskian is \[ W(x)=y_1(x)y_2'(x)-y_1'(x)y_2(x). \] Direct computation confirms \( W \) is never zero for any of Theorem 3.2's three pairs: \( (r_2-r_1)e^{(r_1+r_2)x} \) for distinct roots, \( e^{2rx} \) for a repeated root, \( \beta e^{2\alpha x} \) for complex roots — an exponential (or a nonzero constant times one), never zero.

Let \( g \) be continuous on an interval \( I \), and let \( y_1,y_2,W \) be as in Definition 5.1. Then \[ y_p=-y_1\int\frac{y_2\,g}{aW}\,dx+y_2\int\frac{y_1\,g}{aW}\,dx \] is a particular solution of \( ay''+by'+cy=g(x) \) on \( I \), for any choice of antiderivatives in the two integrals.

Seek \( y_p=u_1y_1+u_2y_2 \) for unknown functions \( u_1,u_2 \) ("varying" what were constants in \( y_c \) — the method's name). Then \( y_p'=u_1'y_1+u_1y_1'+u_2'y_2+u_2y_2' \); impose the constraint \[ u_1'y_1+u_2'y_2=0 \qquad(\ast) \] purely to simplify what follows (there are two unknown functions \( u_1,u_2 \) and so far only one requirement, that \( y_p \) solve the ODE — imposing \( (\ast) \) uses up the spare freedom, and is justified after the fact by producing a genuine solution). With \( (\ast) \), \( y_p'=u_1y_1'+u_2y_2' \), so \( y_p''=u_1'y_1'+u_1y_1''+u_2'y_2'+u_2y_2'' \). Substituting into \( ay_p''+by_p'+cy_p \):

\[ a y_p''+by_p'+cy_p=u_1\big(ay_1''+by_1'+cy_1\big)+u_2\big(ay_2''+by_2'+cy_2\big)+a\big(u_1'y_1'+u_2'y_2'\big)=a\big(u_1'y_1'+u_2'y_2'\big), \] using that \( y_1,y_2 \) solve the homogeneous equation. Setting this equal to \( g(x) \) gives a second relation, \[ u_1'y_1'+u_2'y_2'=\frac{g(x)}{a}\qquad(\ast\ast). \] Together, \( (\ast) \) and \( (\ast\ast) \) are a linear system for \( u_1',u_2' \): \[ \begin{pmatrix}y_1&y_2\\y_1'&y_2'\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}u_1'\\u_2'\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\g/a\end{pmatrix}, \] whose coefficient matrix has determinant \( W(x) \), nonzero by Definition 5.1. Solving (Cramer's rule, or direct elimination): \[ u_1'=-\frac{y_2\,g}{aW},\qquad u_2'=\frac{y_1\,g}{aW}. \] Integrating — any antiderivative works, since only one particular solution is needed — and substituting back into \( y_p=u_1y_1+u_2y_2 \) gives the stated formula.

value.en: From Theorem 3.2 (Chapter 3), get the complementary function's two basis solutions and compute \( W=y_1y_2'-y_1'y_2 \)
\( u_1'=-\dfrac{y_2\,g}{aW} \), \( u_2'=\dfrac{y_1\,g}{aW} \) — using the full forcing \( g(x) \) directly, whatever form it takes
\( u_1=\displaystyle\int u_1'\,dx \), \( u_2=\displaystyle\int u_2'\,dx \) — any antiderivative; the constant of integration can be dropped, since only one particular solution is needed
\( y_p=u_1y_1+u_2y_2 \), then \( y=y_c+y_p \) (Theorem 4.1 still applies) — apply initial conditions the same way as Chapters 3–4 if given

label.en: Worked example 5.A — A forcing term with no trial form

body.en:
Find a particular solution of \( y''+y=\tan x \) (for \( -\pi/2<x<\pi/2 \), where \( \tan x \) is continuous).

Homogeneous: \( r^2+1=0\Rightarrow y_1=\cos x \), \( y_2=\sin x \) (Theorem 3.2, complex case with \( \alpha=0,\beta=1 \)). Wronskian: \( W=\cos x\cos x-({-}\sin x)\sin x=\cos^2x+\sin^2x=1 \).

\( u_1'=-\dfrac{y_2\tan x}{W}=-\sin x\tan x=-\dfrac{\sin^2x}{\cos x}=\cos x-\sec x \) (using \( \sin^2x=1-\cos^2x \)). Integrating: \( u_1=\sin x-\ln|\sec x+\tan x| \).

\( u_2'=\dfrac{y_1\tan x}{W}=\cos x\tan x=\sin x \). Integrating: \( u_2=-\cos x \).

So \[ y_p=u_1y_1+u_2y_2=\big(\sin x-\ln|\sec x+\tan x|\big)\cos x+({-}\cos x)(\sin x)=-\cos x\ln|\sec x+\tan x|, \] the \( \sin x\cos x \) terms cancelling. Chapter 4's method has no trial form for \( \tan x \) at all — this chapter's method needed no trial, just the integral.

label.en: Worked example 5.B — A repeated root, with a forcing term dividing by x

body.en:
Find a particular solution of \( y''-2y'+y=\dfrac{e^x}{x} \) (for \( x>0 \)).

Homogeneous: \( r^2-2r+1=(r-1)^2=0\Rightarrow y_1=e^x \), \( y_2=xe^x \) (repeated root, Theorem 3.2). Wronskian: \( W=e^x(e^x+xe^x)-e^x(xe^x)=e^{2x}(1+x-x)=e^{2x} \).

\( u_1'=-\dfrac{y_2}{W}\cdot\dfrac{e^x}{x}=-\dfrac{xe^x}{e^{2x}}\cdot\dfrac{e^x}{x}=-1 \). Integrating: \( u_1=-x \).

\( u_2'=\dfrac{y_1}{W}\cdot\dfrac{e^x}{x}=\dfrac{e^x}{e^{2x}}\cdot\dfrac{e^x}{x}=\dfrac{1}{x} \). Integrating: \( u_2=\ln x \).

So \[ y_p=u_1y_1+u_2y_2=-xe^x+xe^x\ln x=xe^x(\ln x-1). \]

label.en: Worked example 5.C — Comparing with undetermined coefficients

body.en:
Chapter 4's Worked example 4.B solved \( y''-3y'+2y=e^x \) by undetermined coefficients (with the resonance modification), finding \( y_p=-xe^x \). Solve the same equation by variation of parameters instead, and compare.

\( y_1=e^x \), \( y_2=e^{2x} \) (Theorem 3.2, roots \( 1,2 \)). \( W=e^x(2e^{2x})-e^x(e^{2x})=e^{3x} \).

\( u_1'=-\dfrac{y_2e^x}{W}=-\dfrac{e^{2x}e^x}{e^{3x}}=-1\Rightarrow u_1=-x \). \( u_2'=\dfrac{y_1e^x}{W}=\dfrac{e^xe^x}{e^{3x}}=e^{-x}\Rightarrow u_2=-e^{-x} \).

So \[ y_p=u_1y_1+u_2y_2=-xe^x-e^{-x}e^{2x}=-xe^x-e^x=-(x+1)e^x. \] This differs from Chapter 4's \( -xe^x \) by exactly \( -e^x \) — but \( e^x \) is itself a homogeneous solution (\( y_1 \) above), so by Theorem 4.1 the two answers describe the same general solution family: \( y_c-xe^x \) and \( y_c-(x+1)e^x=y_c-xe^x-e^x \) are identical once \( C_1 \) absorbs the extra \( -e^x \). A particular solution is never unique — only the family \( y=y_c+y_p \) is.

Chapters 3 through 5 now solve every constant-coefficient linear second-order equation in closed form — homogeneous, forced by a polynomial/exponential/trig combination, or forced by anything else continuous at all. What none of these methods handle is a forcing term with a jump or an impulse — a switch flipped at a specific instant, a hammer strike modeled as acting over zero time — exactly the kind of input real control systems and circuits actually receive. The next stage of this track introduces the tool built for exactly that: the Laplace transform, which turns a differential equation into an algebraic one.
